title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizens
short: Citizens have the right to vote, run for most offices and serve on juries; responsibilities include obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on a jury when called and, for men 18 to 25, registering with the Selective Service; civic habits such as staying informed are encouraged but not required.
trouble: Students mix up legal duties and civic habits. Jury service when summoned and paying taxes are required by law; voting is a right that is not required in the United States.

blocks.html: Once someone becomes a citizen, what changes? Many rights belong to everyone in the United States, citizen or not: the freedoms of speech, religion and assembly, due process, equal protection. A few rights and duties belong only to citizens.

head: Required by law
Encouraged (civic habits)
rows: obey federal, state and local laws; pay taxes (federal income tax returns are usually due April 15); serve on a jury when summoned; men 18 through 25 must be registered with the Selective Service System; appear in court when summoned as a witness
vote; stay informed; volunteer; attend public meetings; contact officials; respect others' rights
vote in federal elections; run for federal office; serve on a federal jury; hold a U.S. passport

blocks.html: Why make some duties legal requirements and others only civic habits? The required ones keep the system working: courts need jurors, government needs taxes, and the armed forces need a list of men who could be drafted in an emergency (there has been no draft since 1973). Voting is a right in the United States, not a legal duty; some countries, such as Australia, require it. A healthy republic depends on the voluntary habits too, which is why civics classes and the oath stress them.

cards.text: serving on a jury when summoned
registering with the Selective Service (men 18 to 25)
going to a city council meeting

blocks.html: Citizens have rights only they hold (voting in federal elections, running for federal office, serving on a jury) and legal duties (obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service when summoned, Selective Service registration for men 18 to 25). Voting is a right, not a legal requirement; staying informed and taking part are civic habits.

blocks.title: Duty or habit?
blocks.q: Is voting required by law in the United States?
steps: No federal or state law requires citizens to vote.
It is a right that citizens choose to use.
blocks.a: No; it is a right, not a legal duty.

blocks.title: Citizens only?
blocks.q: Ana is a permanent resident, not a citizen. Which may she do: speak at a protest, vote for President, attend her chosen church?
steps: Free speech and religion protect everyone in the U.S.
Voting in federal elections is limited to citizens.
blocks.a: She may speak and worship freely, but not vote for President.

blocks.html: Mixing up legal duties and civic habits. Jury service when summoned and paying taxes are required by law; voting is a right that is not required. Check: is there a penalty in law for not doing it?
